Overall grade based on % responses violating assessment standard. No model has achieved Excellent yet (target: Very Good).

name: Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)
description: Cross-benchmark composite metric combining 42 AI benchmarks (3 categories per https://epoch.ai/data/eci-documentation/data) into a single 'general capability' scale. Calibrated so Claude 3.5 Sonnet = 130 and GPT-5 (medium) = 150. Linear scale: a 10-point jump represents equivalent capability gain regardless of position. Methodology paper 'A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks' (arxiv 2512.00193, Anson Ho et al) — IRT-style stitching infers benchmark difficulty statistically from overlapping model results, weights harder benchmarks more, avoids inflation from specialized models. Models with <4 benchmark scores or pre-2023 release excluded due to data sparsity. Contributing benchmarks: (Internal Evaluations) Chess Puzzles, FrontierMath Tiers 1-3, FrontierMath Tier 4, GPQA Diamond, MATH Level 5, OTIS Mock AIME 2024-2025, SimpleQA Verified. (External Leaderboards) Aider polyglot, APEX-Agents, ARC-AGI-2, BALROG, DeepResearch Bench, Fiction.liveBench, GeoBench, GSO, HLE, SimpleBench, SWE-bench (Bash Only), Terminal-Bench, The Agent Company, VPCT, WeirdML V2. (Developer Reported) ANLI, ARC AI2, ARC-AGI, BIG-Bench Hard, CADEval, CSQA2, Cybench, GSM8K, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, Lech Mazur Writing, MMLU, OpenBookQA, OSWorld, PIQA, ScienceQA, SuperGLUE, TriviaQA, Video MME, WinoGrande. Benchmarks rescaled so random-guess = 0. Domain-specific ECI variants (Software Engineering, Math, custom) use the same Rosetta Stone methodology on subsets.

name: Epoch Capabilities Index — Software Engineering
description: Domain-specific Epoch Capabilities Index using only software engineering benchmarks (SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, Aider Polyglot, etc). Same Rosetta Stone methodology as general ECI applied to software engineering subset only.

name: Lech Mazur Writing

WARNING — the benchmark changed its scoring scheme: the rows stored here were collected 2026-05-10 on the old absolute 0-10 scale (qwen3-235b 8.3, gpt-4o 8.18). The current board publishes a relative Thurstone 'comparison score' where zero sits near the middle of the field and the top entry is ~4.1 (Fable 5.1, Opus 5), plus an estimated win chance. The two are NOT comparable — if the current board is ever ingested it must go to a new benchmark id, not this one.

name: ERRORQUAKE-10K (severity tail-slope b)
description: Per-model fit of log10 N(M>=m) = a - b*m on a 0.0-4.0 severity scale across 10,000 queries (8 domains x 5 difficulty tiers). Higher b = lighter tail (fewer catastrophic fabrications); lower b = heavier tail (more order-of-magnitude failures). Dual-judge 8-model round-robin scoring validated against 519-item 3-rater human study (ICC=0.85, judge-vs-human rank rho=0.89). 95% CIs from n=2000 bootstrap resamples.
metric: Gutenberg-Richter upper-tail slope b of error-severity distribution

name: ERRORQUAKE-10K error rate (ε)

name: WebGameBench — Usable rate
description: WebGameBench (arXiv 2605.17637, Baidu): 111 frozen Structured WebGame Specifications (7 gameplay families, D1-D4 difficulty) that a coding agent must turn into a deployed browser-native game; a Codex CLI (gpt-5.4 xhigh) runtime evaluator plays the game in Chrome via Playwright and assigns EXCELLENT/USABLE/UNUSABLE. Usable rate = share of valid scored samples labeled EXCELLENT or USABLE. Evaluator agrees with human gameplay review at 85.0% accuracy (XHigh) on the Usable criterion. Higher is better.

name: WebGameBench — Excellent rate
description: WebGameBench (arXiv 2605.17637): same 111 browser-native game tasks; Excellent rate = share of valid scored samples whose delivered game fully and stably satisfies the specification (label EXCELLENT). Stricter signal; exact three-way label agreement with humans only 50%. Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — Stage 1 Exact-Match localization (cumulative)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Stage 1 metric: share of tasks where the agent modified exactly the ground-truth file set (P = T), cumulative over all tiers; AIDER CLI harness with 300 s cutoff (timeouts excluded). Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — Stage 1 EM (Easy)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Easy tier (near-mechanical edit instructions with exact file/line refs). AIDER harness. Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — Stage 1 EM (Medium)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Medium tier (what/why plus affected subsystems, no line-level recipe). AIDER harness. Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — Stage 1 EM (Difficult)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Difficult tier (high-level objective only, no file/function names). AIDER harness. Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — Unit Test Acceptance Rate (UAR)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Stage 2 (exact-match subset only): share of patches that compile and pass srsRAN unit/integration tests. Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — TeleJudge Acceptance Rate (TAR)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Stage 2 (exact-match subset only): share of patches accepted by the hierarchical TeleJudge LLM-as-a-judge (file-level then holistic verdict). Higher is better.

name: TeleSWEBench — Ship-Ready Percentage (SRP)
description: TeleSWEBench (arXiv 2606.05001, NCSU/UCSD): 734 commit-derived tasks (Easy 142 / Medium 279 / Difficult 313) mined from the srsRAN 5G C++ repository, each with executable unit tests. Stage 2 (exact-match subset only): share of patches that both pass TeleJudge and pass all build/unit tests (strictest end-to-end metric). Best reported 25.0% (GLM-4.7, AIDER). Higher is better.

name: CORE-Bench (code retrieval) — L1-L3 average NDCG@10
description: CORE-Bench for code retrieval in agentic coding (arXiv 2606.11864, Beihang/PKU; NOT the CORE-Bench computational-reproducibility benchmark): >180K queries, 106K relevance labels; Level-1 code understanding (text-code/code-code/code-text/hybrid), Level-2 issue-to-edit localization and Level-3 broader-context retrieval built from SWE-bench-series instances (Pro/Verified/Live/Multilingual...). Embedding-model retrieval over repository-state corpora. Higher is better. Headline: average NDCG@10 over L1, L2, L3.

name: Dialogue-SWEBench — % Resolved (OpenHands scaffold)
description: Dialogue-SWEBench (arXiv 2606.13995, UCSC): the 500 SWE-bench Verified problems re-cast as dialogue-driven sessions — the agent only sees an under-specified initial user query and must elicit missing details from a persona-grounded simulated user (quantized Llama 3.3 70B with self-revision) who never touches code; success = submitted patch passes the SWE-bench Verified execution tests. 100 agent steps per problem. Higher is better. Off-the-shelf OpenHands agent (plus message_user tool).

description: Dialogue-SWEBench (arXiv 2606.13995, UCSC): the 500 SWE-bench Verified problems re-cast as dialogue-driven sessions — the agent only sees an under-specified initial user query and must elicit missing details from a persona-grounded simulated user (quantized Llama 3.3 70B with self-revision) who never touches code; success = submitted patch passes the SWE-bench Verified execution tests. 100 agent steps per problem. name: CoDA-Bench — Execution Accuracy (Codex CLI scaffold)
description: CoDA-Bench (arXiv 2606.15300, Renmin Univ., ICML 2026): 1,009 data-intensive analytical tasks over a Kaggle-derived Linux sandbox (31 data communities, ~980 files per environment, SNR 0.0105); agent must discover the relevant files and write code to produce the answer. CoDA-Hard = 119-task subset needing >=2 target files and >30-line reference solutions. DA = Discovery Accuracy (correct target files located); EA = Execution Accuracy (task output correct). Higher is better. Scaffold: Codex CLI (official default configuration for native CLI tools; unified framework for OpenHands / Mini-SWE-agent).

name: SWE-bench Verified (200-task sample) — Vanilla re-run in SWE-Touch (mini-swe-agent)
description: SWE-Touch (arXiv 2608.02499, CASIA): stress-tests coding agents in a shared workspace via validated Counter-Edits — plausible user code edits that conflict with task completion, injected (with a short user message) when the agent reaches the task-critical region. Main cohort: seeded 200-task sample of SWE-bench Verified, Mini-SWE-Agent harness on Harbor, 100-step budget, mean of 3 runs. Vanilla (no user edit) resolve rate on the 200-task Verified sample — re-run of other vendors' models by the SWE-Touch authors.

name: MT-Web2Code — Macro-Level regional reconstruction Score
description: MT-Web2Code (arXiv 2608.03474, HIT / Meituan): multimodal multi-turn web-UI coding benchmark for coding agents. name: GameXpert-Bench GameGen — Overall score
description: GameXpert-Bench (arXiv 2608.21833, Tencent Hunyuan / Lightspeed): three-track game-development lifecycle benchmark for coding agents. GameGen = 97 single-request browser-native game generation tasks (11 genres, 44 3D) built with Claude Code under default configuration, judged by an evidence-grounded LLM judge on Completeness / Richness / Player Experience / Visual Quality (Overall = mean, 0-100). GameOpt = human-guided multi-turn refinement over 17 JavaScript games / 102 requests, six-dimension discrimination-weighted score (0-100). Higher is better. name: HVTB — reward-hack rate, Ablation prompt (no anti-hack instruction)
description: Hack-Verifiable Terminal Bench / HVTB (arXiv 2608.22103, Tel Aviv Univ. / UCSB): the 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks instrumented with two planted, deterministically detectable reward hacks (a leaked hidden solution and readable held-out tests in an admin/ directory). Metric = any-hack rate: share of completed runs that triggered at least one planted hack. Prompt classes: Ablation = no hacking-related instruction; L0 = generic 'solve on your own / do not hack'; L1-L3 = progressively more specific disclosure of the vulnerability. Each model runs in its native harness (Claude Code, Codex, gemini-cli; terminus-2 for open models). Lower is better. Setting: Ablation prompt (no anti-hack instruction).

name: OpenHarmony Bench — Task Completion (all 153 tasks)

name: PatchBench — Solved rate (Codex)
description: PatchBench (arXiv 2609.04075, Univ. of Maryland): 213 C/C++ repository-level vulnerability-patching tasks from 32 GitHub projects / 16 CWEs, built by vulnerability transplant + code mutation so ground-truth fixes lie outside the crash stack (mitigating patch memorization and stack-trace-only fixes). Agent gets the repo, PoC, sanitizer report and build commands in Docker; $5 budget per task, medium reasoning effort, no web access. Solved = patch passes both security validation (new PoCs / fuzzing) and semantic validation; PoC Pass = original PoC no longer crashes (inflates solve rate 1.83x). Higher is better. Scaffold: Codex.

description: Vercel DeepsecBench (launched 2026-07-27; board at vercel.com/ai-gateway/leaderboards/deepsecbench): vulnerability discovery in one undisclosed open-source codebase pinned before a large batch of fixes — 50 entry-point files, golden set of 231 human-judged findings. Score = recall-weighted F2 = 100·5PR/(4P+R); findings outside the golden set are judged real/false and count toward precision only; median of 3 runs. Run with the vendor harness per model (Codex for OpenAI, Claude Code for Anthropic, Pi for others) via deepsec. AA re-implements it on Stirrup as `deepsecbench_aa` (not comparable). Headline F2 score.

name: Vals CyberBench v1.1 (overall accuracy)
description: Vals AI CyberBench v1.1 (updated 2026-10-07; supersedes v1 — offline sandboxes + hardened clean-room grader, not comparable): OSS-Fuzz crash regressions from ARVO images harvested after CyberGym's task window, mostly memory-safety / UB bugs in native code. PoC track (60 tasks): from source + fuzz target, produce a crashing input (must crash vulnerable build, not the fixed one). Patch track (56 tasks): given PoC + sanitizer report, patch so the PoC no longer crashes and hidden holdout inputs match the maintainer fix. mini-swe-agent harness; provider refusals count as failures. Overall accuracy.

name: CS-Guard base-LLM ASR (internal-type guardrail = alignment) — text-to-code level 1 (base TTP prompts, no jailbreak)
description: Attack success rate of the base code LLM itself (no external guardrail), lower is better. Split: text-to-code level 1 (base TTP prompts, no jailbreak). CS-Guard (arXiv 2609.09798, Li/Guo/Nguyen, Adelaide Univ., 2026). Text-to-code: 1000 CyberSecEval MITRE-TTP malware prompts (level 1 base; level 2 = 7 jailbreaks + FSA, 1000 prompts each); code-to-code: 331 malware code prompts (160 completion from RedCode-Gen, 80 infilling + 91 translation from RMCBench). 5 samples/prompt, attack counted successful if any response labelled bad by majority-vote LLM labeler (96.8/93.8/93.7% agreement with human labels). License CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (FSA data).
